claims.text: Optimizing the noble-to-base metal ratio in a high-entropy alloy enhances charge transfer.
Base metals transfer electrons to noble-metal sites.
Charge transfer from base metals to noble-metal sites shifts the d-band center.
The resulting d-band-center shift tunes the binding energies of reaction intermediates toward an optimum.
Suitable intermediate binding energies lower barriers for key elementary steps and facilitate reaction kinetics.
Avoiding excessively strong adsorption reduces surface poisoning, including possible carbon deposition.
Composition-dependent electronic and adsorbate-binding effects can enhance catalytic activity in compositionally complex catalysts.
The proposed ratio-induced electronic modulation improves catalyst durability.
The initial near-equiatomic high-entropy alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
Changing the noble-to-base metal ratio produces spatial isolation of noble-metal sites.
Interfacial oxygen vacancies arise from charge-transfer effects between the alloy components.
An optimized noble-to-base metal ratio will lower activation energy relative to a near-equiatomic baseline.
An optimized noble-to-base metal ratio will increase reaction yield or current density relative to a near-equiatomic baseline.
An optimized noble-to-base metal ratio will increase operational stability relative to a near-equiatomic baseline.
The near-equiatomic baseline has less pronounced charge transfer and d-band shifting than the optimized composition.
The hypothesis is intended to apply when morphology and support interactions remain constant and mass transport does not limit the measured kinetics.
Failure to observe a statistically significant ratio-dependent decrease in activation energy or increase in yield, current density, or durability would falsify the hypothesis.
